topics.title: HTTP caching — no-cache, no-store, ETag, and immutable assets.
topics.html:
HTTP caching has two separate questions: may the response be stored, and may the stored response be reused without checking with the server?

  • no-store tells caches not to store the response. It does not erase copies that were stored under an earlier policy.
  • no-cache allows storage but requires validation before reuse. It does not mean “never cache.”
  • An ETag is a validator. A matching If-None-Match request can receive a 304 response so the cached body can be reused.
  • Fingerprint-named assets can have a long lifetime and immutable, because changed bytes receive a different URL.

Keep the HTML entry point discoverably fresh so it can reference new asset hashes. For personalized responses, deliberately control shared-cache storage and identity variation; a user-specific query key in React does not configure a CDN cache.

# HTML entry point: store, but validate before reuse
Cache-Control: no-cache
ETag: "html-release-42"

# Content-hashed public asset: /assets/app.8a6b32.js
Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable

# A response that must not be stored
Cache-Control: no-store

# Conditional request for the stored HTML
If-None-Match: "html-release-42"
# Unchanged representation: server responds 304 Not Modified
In plain words

I choose a policy for each kind of resource. Stable hashed files can be reused for a long time; the HTML that points to them must discover a new release. no-cache means check before reuse, while no-store means do not store this response.

Why can a correct deploy still show an old application?
Different layers may retain different resources: the browser HTTP cache, a service worker, a CDN, and an application cache are independent. I inspect the actual response headers and asset URLs before blaming React.
Does private mean encrypted or accessible only after authentication?
No. It controls shared-cache storage. HTTPS, authentication, authorization, and the application’s data exposure are separate concerns.
Official references
  • MDN: HTTP caching
  • MDN: Cache-Control

topics.title: CORS and cookies — why can a successful response still be blocked?
topics.html:
CORS controls whether browser JavaScript can read a cross-origin response. An HTTP 200 in the network panel does not prove that the response satisfies that policy.

  • A preflight asks whether the method and request headers are allowed. JSON content types and many non-simple methods or headers trigger it.
  • For credentialed cross-origin requests, configure the request's credentials mode and return an explicitly allowed origin plus Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true.
  • Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * cannot be used to expose a credentialed response. Validate the origin against an allowlist rather than blindly reflecting it.
  • Cookie delivery still follows SameSite rules, Secure requirements, and browser restrictions. Enabling CORS does not override those rules.

Return the appropriate CORS headers on error responses too. Otherwise a useful application error can appear to the client as an unreadable network failure. CORS does not replace authentication, authorization, or CSRF defenses.

const response = await fetch('https://api.example.com/profile', {
  method: 'PATCH',
  credentials: 'include',
  headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
  body: JSON.stringify({ displayName: 'Alex' }),
});
if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${response.status}`);

// API response policy for an explicitly allowed app origin:
// Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://app.example.com
// Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true
// Vary: Origin
// Preflight also permits PATCH and the Content-Type request header.
In plain words

A server can complete the request while the browser refuses to expose the response. I inspect the origin, the preflight, the actual response headers, and the cookie policy as separate parts of the problem.

Will mode: "no-cors" fix an API request?
It normally gives JavaScript an opaque response whose status and body cannot be read, and restricts the request shape. It is not a way to turn an incompatible API into a normal readable JSON endpoint.
Why does the same request work in a server process or an API client?
The browser enforces the same-origin policy and CORS. A non-browser HTTP client is not evidence that the browser policy is configured correctly.
Official references
  • MDN: CORS
  • MDN: Access-Control-Allow-Credentials
  • MDN: Set-Cookie

topics.title: Query keys and invalidation — why does the UI show another filter’s data?
topics.html:
A query key identifies cached server data. Include the inputs that change the result: the resource, workspace or user scope, filters, sorting, and pagination state.

  • The query function and key must describe the same request. Changing a variable captured by the function does not make it part of the key automatically.
  • Organize keys in prefixes so a successful mutation can invalidate the relevant family of lists or details.
  • staleTime controls freshness. gcTime controls how long unused data can remain before garbage collection; they solve different problems.
  • For normal enabled queries, invalidation marks matching data stale and can refetch active consumers. Explicitly disabled or static queries have different rules.

Clear or appropriately scope cached data when switching identities. “The data was in the cache” is not proof that it belongs to the current user or selected workspace.

const projects = useQuery({
  queryKey: ['projects', workspaceId, { status }],
  queryFn: async ({ signal }) => {
    const params = new URLSearchParams({ status });
    const response = await fetch(
      `/api/workspaces/${encodeURIComponent(workspaceId)}/projects?${params}`,
      { signal },
    );
    if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${response.status}`);
    return response.json(); // Validate this boundary in the application.
  },
  staleTime: 30_000,
});

// After a successful change in this workspace:
await queryClient.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: ['projects', workspaceId] });
In plain words

A cache entry needs the same identity as the request it represents. If two filters or workspaces share a key, the cache cannot distinguish them. I design keys and mutation invalidation together.

Should every successful mutation invalidate the entire cache?
Usually not. Update a known detail value or invalidate the affected key family. Broad invalidation creates avoidable network work and can disrupt unrelated screens.
Is staleTime: Infinity identical to static freshness?
No. Infinity can still be invalidated. TanStack Query’s static setting is stricter and blocks this normal invalidation behavior; choose it only when that lifetime guarantee matches the application.
Official references
  • TanStack Query: query keys
  • TanStack Query: invalidation
  • TanStack Query: important defaults

topics.title: Offset vs cursor pagination — how do you keep a changing feed consistent?
topics.html:
Offset pagination describes a position: skip a number of rows and take the next page. Cursor pagination continues from a server-defined boundary in an ordering.

  • Offsets are convenient for page numbers and direct jumps. Inserts or removals before the current offset can shift items between requests.
  • A cursor is usually opaque to the client. It must preserve the server’s ordering and filtering context; the UI should not invent or increment it.
  • Use deterministic ordering with a tie-breaker, such as creation time plus a unique ID. A timestamp alone may not distinguish two records.
  • When a filter or sort changes, reset the cursor and use a matching cache key. Do not append results from the old query into the new feed.

A cursor alone does not freeze a live dataset. Decide whether the API promises snapshot consistency or a best-effort moving feed, and how the client handles repeated IDs, deleted entries, and newly arriving items.

async function loadNextPage({ cursor, status, signal }) {
  const params = new URLSearchParams({ status, limit: '20' });
  if (cursor !== null) params.set('after', cursor);

  const response = await fetch(`/api/activity?${params}`, { signal });
  if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${response.status}`);
  return response.json();
  // Contract: { items, nextCursor: string | null }.
  // Validate the payload before appending it to application state.
}
In plain words

An offset says where to start counting. A cursor says where to continue in a particular ordered query. For a live feed I also need a clear consistency contract and stable item identities, not just a Load more button.

Can I go directly to page 50 with a cursor?
Not automatically. A cursor API may require traversing boundaries or a separate lookup mechanism. That trade-off matters when the product needs random page access rather than a continuous feed.
Is endless scrolling always the best UI?
No. Consider keyboard access, restoring position after navigation, reaching the footer, and the user’s need to compare or bookmark results. Explicit pagination or Load more may fit better.
Official references
  • GitHub: cursor pagination
  • TanStack Query: paginated queries

topics.title: Safe retries and idempotency — what if the server saved it but the response was lost?
topics.html:
A timeout does not prove that the server did nothing. The request may have completed and only its response may have been lost. Blindly repeating a write can create a second operation.

  • HTTP defines idempotency by the intended server-side effect of repeated identical requests, not by identical response codes. DELETE can remain idempotent even when a later request returns a different status.
  • POST is not automatically idempotent. An API can implement an explicit idempotency-key contract.
  • Create the operation ID once and reuse it for retries of that same logical action. A fresh key for every retry defeats deduplication.
  • The server must enforce the contract, including its key scope, payload-conflict behavior, concurrency handling, and retention window.

Retry only failures the API defines as retryable, with bounded backoff and appropriate handling of Retry-After. A disabled submit button helps the UI but cannot protect against duplicate delivery or another client.

// Keep this object for the lifetime of one logical submission.
const operation = {
  id: crypto.randomUUID(),
  payload: { productId: 'book-42', quantity: 1 },
};

async function submitOrder(operation) {
  const response = await fetch('/api/orders', {
    method: 'POST',
    headers: {
      'Content-Type': 'application/json',
      'Idempotency-Key': operation.id,
    },
    body: JSON.stringify(operation.payload),
  });
  if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${response.status}`);
  return response.json();
}
// This works only if the API implements this header's contract.
In plain words

I distinguish an unknown outcome from a confirmed failure. For a retryable write, the client keeps the same logical operation ID and the server makes repeated delivery safe. The transport alone cannot promise exactly-once behavior.

Can I reuse one idempotency key forever?
No. Different logical operations need different IDs. The API also defines expiration and whether reusing a key with a changed payload is rejected; a key is not a permanent substitute for domain-level uniqueness.
Should validation errors be retried automatically?
Usually not: repeating unchanged invalid input will not help. Separate retryable transport or service failures from a response that requires the user or application to change the request.
Official references
  • MDN: HTTP request methods
  • Stripe: idempotent request contract

topics.title: Polling, SSE, or WebSocket — what does a real-time screen actually need?
topics.html:
Choose the transport from direction, latency, infrastructure, and recovery needs. A persistent connection is not automatically the simplest or most reliable design.

  • Polling is a useful baseline when updates are infrequent. Avoid overlapping requests and pause or reduce work when the view is inactive.
  • Server-sent events provide a server-to-client text stream over HTTP. Native EventSource includes reconnect behavior and supports event IDs for a server-defined resume protocol.
  • WebSocket supports bidirectional messages. The application still needs authentication, reconnect rules, message validation, and recovery after a gap.
  • The classic browser WebSocket API does not provide automatic receive-side backpressure. A producer can overwhelm a slow consumer, so bound work and design a recovery or coalescing policy.

Transport delivery is not domain consistency. Use event identities or versions, deduplicate where required, and fetch a fresh snapshot when incremental history can no longer be resumed safely.

function subscribeToUpdates(onMessage) {
  const source = new EventSource('/api/events');

  source.onmessage = event => {
    onMessage({ id: event.lastEventId, raw: event.data });
  };

  // The caller validates the payload and applies its ordering policy.
  // Native EventSource retries recoverable connection failures.
  return () => source.close();
}

// In a component, return this cleanup from the subscription Effect.
In plain words

For one-way notifications, SSE may cover the requirement with less protocol work. I use WebSocket when the application needs its bidirectional behavior, and in either case I define what happens after disconnects, duplicate events, and missing history.

Can native EventSource set any custom authorization header?
Its browser constructor does not expose an arbitrary headers option. Choose an authentication design it supports, or a deliberate streaming-fetch client, and account for credential and CORS rules.
Does reconnecting guarantee that no update was missed?
No. The server needs a replay or snapshot protocol. A resumed connection without a consistent event history can leave the UI looking live while its state is incomplete.
Official references
  • MDN: server-sent events
  • MDN: WebSocket API
